---
title: "Dropout"
description: "A regularization technique that randomly disables units during neural-network training."
term: "Dropout"
letter: "D"
category: "Deep Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Dropout randomly omits some neural-network units during training. This
discourages the network from relying too heavily on a small set of
activations and can help reduce overfitting.

## Technical explanation

During training, dropout samples a mask that sets selected activations
to zero. In inverted dropout, retained activations are scaled during
training so that their expected magnitude is consistent. At inference,
dropout is typically disabled. The dropout rate and placement are
architecture-dependent.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Dropout can regularize some models, but its effect depends on architecture,
data, and other regularization methods. Correct training and inference
modes are necessary for the intended behaviour.

## How it works

For activation $h_i$, dropout applies a random mask $m_i$ and, with
inverted scaling, produces $\tilde{h}_i = \frac{m_i h_i}{1-p}$ during
training, where $p$ is the drop probability and $m_i$ is zero with
probability $p$. At evaluation time the layer passes activations through.

## Practical example

A dense classifier can include dropout between hidden layers during
training. When evaluating or serving the model, the framework switches
to inference mode so activations are no longer randomly dropped.

## Common misconceptions

- Dropout does not mean permanently deleting neurons or parameters.
- Applying dropout during evaluation can make predictions stochastic and
  inconsistent with standard inference.
- Dropout is not always beneficial, especially when other model or data
  choices already control overfitting.
